messages.subject: Threshold genetic distance
messages.body_plain:
Dear Zhian,

I am using poppr to analysis the results of  a MLVA in bacteria and the final aim is basically dividing these bacteria into different clusters, according to their genetic distance.
I know that part of these bacteria have already been classified into 5 different biovars, but my dataset contains isolates not previously characterized.
My idea is to first use these already classified isolates to define a threshold distance below which they belong to the same cluster. After that, I want to apply this cutoff to the whole dataset and divide them into (possibly) more than 5 clusters.

After clone-correct the dataset, I used mlg.filter with Bruvo's distance and the three different alghoritm to define a cutoff threshold to then collapse the MLGs into MLLs and here some questions have arisen:

1)  I used fraction set to 1, to calculate the cutoff among the whole threshold vector coming from filter_stats. Why there is even the possibility to set 0.5?
2)  Do MLLs correspond to clusters, as defined by clustering algorithms like the K-means or Hierarchical clustering?
3)  By using the three different algorithms (nearest, farthest, UPGMA) I get obviously different cuffoff and thus, different MLLs (from a maximum of 18 to 12). Is there any reason why choosing one or another?
4)  Can I then use this cutoff value in a Hierarchical clustering like hclust? If I got it right, the height in the hclust dendrogram is not based on Bruvo's distance but on the cophenetic distance and thus I cannot used it there.
     Is there another function where i can use this poppr threshold to define clusters?
5)  Or maybe my questions (and the aim) has already been satisfed by mlg.filters and thus, my question 2?

I hope I explain my self. There are too many options, too many discordant possibilties and results which confuse me a lot!

Silvia

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Threshold genetic distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Silvia,

I'm assuming your MLVA markers can be represented by a stepwise mutation model of tandem repeats.

> 1)  I used fraction set to 1, to calculate the cutoff among the whole threshold vector coming from filter_stats. Why there is even the possibility to set 0.5?

Because the function is designed to be flexible for any distance, not just Bruvo.

> 2)  Do MLLs correspond to clusters, as defined by clustering algorithms like the K-means or Hierarchical clustering?

The MLLs are clustered by hierarchical clustering as described in the second poppr paper (doi:10.3389/fgene.2015.00208 <https://doi.org/10.3389/fgene.2015.00208>).

> 3)  By using the three different algorithms (nearest, farthest, UPGMA) I get obviously different cuffoff and thus, different MLLs (from a maximum of 18 to 12). Is there any reason why choosing one or another?

I think this is really dependent on your system. The algorithms behave as mentioned in the second poppr paper (linked above). I made some animations showing their progress in the supplementary materials (mapped on to UPGMA trees):

Nearest: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/grunwaldlab/supplementary-poppr-2.0/blob/master/images/upgma_nearest.html
UPGMA: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/grunwaldlab/supplementary-poppr-2.0/blob/master/images/upgma_average.html
Farthest: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/grunwaldlab/supplementary-poppr-2.0/blob/master/images/upgma_farthest.html

> 4)  Can I then use this cutoff value in a Hierarchical clustering like hclust? If I got it right, the height in the hclust dendrogram is not based on Bruvo's distance but on the cophenetic distance and thus I cannot used it there.
>      Is there another function where i can use this poppr threshold to define clusters?

If the hclust dendrogram is based off of Bruvo's distance then, yes, you can use that cutoff value (but only from the UPGMA algorithm). Another method to define clusters without using distance is to use adegenet::find.clusters() or adegenet::snapclust(). These use multivariate methods to assign populations.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Hello Ram,

I haven't needed to subset my data yet because I haven't found calculations to be running too slowly on my genind object (~16k SNPs). If you're running into long computation times, you could try taking a random subset of SNPs (pretty easy using vcflib, probably ways of doing it in R too...), or you could try pulling out the PCA loadings to find the most contributing alleles. I haven't tried this yet, but it's explained in the adegenet DAPC tutorial (http://adegenet.r-forge.r-project.org/files/tutorial-dapc.pdf) section 3.4.

Good luck!

Evan

messages.subject: Poppr 2.8.3 has been released!
messages.body_plain:
Hello friends,

Poppr version 2.8.3 has been released on CRAN and will be built for windows and macOS in the coming days. This contains a bug fix for a corner case in read.genalex and a contribution from Frédéric Chevalier, who kindly added a feature that made the minimum spanning networks look better.

You can read about the changes here: https://github.com/grunwaldlab/poppr/releases/tag/v.2.8.3

And, like a doofus, I forgot to include the NEWS file in the official CRAN release, but you can always keep up-to-date with the changes here: https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/news/index.html

Cheers,
Zhian

P.S. I haven't been so good at announcing the new updates and I promise to get better at that.

messages.subject: Re: k-mean clustering
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ram,

Both find.clusters and dapc are from the adegenet package and you can find more information about them here: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/wiki/Tutorials.

In short, both of these methods first calculate principal components from the allele dosage matrix. The find.clusters function performs K-means clustering, which finds ad-hoc clusters while dapc attempts to perform discriminant analysis based on known populations (in this case, the results of K-means clustering are used as the 'populations', for a more in-depth detailing of DAPC, see https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/DAPC.html and https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/gbs_analysis.html#dapc).

The "LD" in the plot refers to "Linear Discriminant Axis", which are similar to Principal Component Axes, but these take into account the group membership.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

messages.subject: Most appropriate distance metric for mixed-ploidy (diploid and polyploid) SNP data?
messages.subject_clean: Most appropriate distance metric for mixed-ploidy (diploid and polyploid) SNP data?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Poppr's!

I've been using Poppr successfully (I hope) to look at population structure in my mixed-ploidy SNP data by importing each ploidy level (diploid, triploid, and tetraploid) into a separate genind object and then pooling into a combined genind. This has allowed me to detect clonality and MLGs (my polyploids are also asexual), as well as use PCA/DAPC and K-means clustering. I know that multivariate approaches can allow me to bypass some of the assumption-breaking aspects of my data, but I would now like to construct some trees, calculate population differentiation statistics, and look at pair-wise distances between individuals. From what I can tell, all of these require some sort of distance matrix, of which I know Poppr offers several options. However, according to "The Analysis of Polyploid Genetic Data" (Meirmans et al 2018), all of the distance metrics they evaluated are biased for mixed ploidy analyses, and should be avoided (but apparently the relatedness coefficients are unbiased?). On the other hand, Meirmans and Liu (2018) suggest using squared Euclidian distances to calculate AMOVA and rho, which is supposed to be OK for mixed-ploidy datasets. I understand that the theory from this paper been incorporated into Poppr in the poppr.amova() function, which is great. All of that said, I have a few questions:

1) Is there a suitable distance metric I can use in Poppr to look at pairwise differences between individuals in my mixed-ploidy dataset? I'd mainly like to use this to create a distance tree to assess the number of origins of asexuality in my species (by looking at asexual lineages nested with sexual populations on the tree). I cannot use Bruvo distance as I do not have microsatellite data, and Meirmans et al 2018 reported that Bruvo distance is biased anyways...If not, is there a way to calculate "relatedness coefficients" in Poppr as discussed in Meirmans et al 2018?

2) Is it possible to do a pairwise AMOVA between all of the populations in my dataset in Poppr? I saw that there was an open issue somewhere on github for this, but I'm not sure if it's been implemented (or whether there's a workaround to do it manually...).

3) This is only semi-related to the above topic, but a few of the analyses I've attempted to do requires me to convert my genind to genpop. However, I receive an error from genind2genpop that "conversion to genpop not supported for varying ploidy". Is there any workaround for this?

Thanks in advance for any advice you may have!

Evan
